{{short description|American theoretical physicist (born 1955)}}
'''Gary T. Horowitz''' (born April 14, 1955 in [[Washington, D.C.]]) is an American theoretical physicist who works on [[string theory]] and [[quantum gravity]].

==Biography==
Horowitz studied at [[Princeton University]] (Bachelor 1976) and obtained his Ph.D. in 1979 at the [[University of Chicago]] with [[Robert Geroch]].  Subsequently, he was a post-doc at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] and [[Oxford University]] (as a NATO Fellow). In 1981-1983 he worked as an Einstein Fellow at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]. He became an assistant professor in 1983, associate professor in 1986, and finally professor in 1990 at the University of California at Santa Barbara.

Horowitz investigates gravitational phenomena, such as black holes, in string theory.  In the 1990s, he worked with, among others, [[Andrew Strominger]]<ref name="Horowitz Strominger p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Horowitz | first1=Gary | last2=Strominger | first2=Andrew | title=Counting States of Near-Extremal Black Holes | journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. | year=1996 | volume=77 | issue=12 | pages=2368–2371 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.2368 | pmid=10061936 | arxiv=hep-th/9602051 | bibcode=1996PhRvL..77.2368H | s2cid=633266 }}</ref> and [[Joseph Polchinski]] showing that string theory provides a description of the quantum microstates of certain black holes (following earlier work of Strominger and [[Cumrun Vafa]]).<ref>For  general black holes, one can only show the proportionality of the logarithm of the number of string states to the surface area (which corresponds to the entropy), {{cite journal |arxiv=hep-th/9612146|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.55.6189 |title=Correspondence principle for black holes and strings |year=1997 |last1=Horowitz |first1=Gary T. |last2=Polchinski |first2=Joseph |journal=Physical Review D |volume=55 |issue=10 |pages=6189–6197 |bibcode=1997PhRvD..55.6189H |s2cid=13134692 }}</ref>

In 1985 Horowitz published an influential paper with [[Philip Candelas]], [[Andrew Strominger]] and [[Edward Witten]] on the compactification of superstrings in Calabi-Yau spaces.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/0550-3213(85)90602-9 | title=Vacuum configurations for superstrings | year=1985 | last1=Candelas | first1=P. | last2=Horowitz | first2=Gary T. | last3=Strominger | first3=Andrew | last4=Witten | first4=Edward | journal=Nuclear Physics B | volume=258 | pages=46–74 | bibcode=1985NuPhB.258...46C }}</ref> In the early 1990s, Horowitz and Strominger found black [[brane]] solutions in string theory.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/0550-3213(91)90440-9 | title=Black strings and p-branes | year=1991 | last1=Horowitz | first1=Gary T. | last2=Strominger | first2=Andrew | journal=Nuclear Physics B | volume=360 | issue=1 | pages=197–209 | bibcode=1991NuPhB.360..197H }}</ref> Horowitz also works on the [[AdS/CFT correspondence]] and (together with Sean Hartnoll and Chris Herzog) discovered holographic [[superconductors]].<ref>{{cite book | arxiv=1002.1722 | doi=10.1007/978-3-642-04864-7_10 | chapter=Introduction to Holographic Superconductors | title=From Gravity to Thermal Gauge Theories: The AdS/CFT Correspondence | series=Lecture Notes in Physics | year=2011 | last1=Horowitz | first1=Gary T. | volume=828 | pages=313–347 | isbn=978-3-642-04863-0 | s2cid=118582465 }}</ref>

In 1982 Horowitz and M. Perry won first prize in the Gravity Research Foundation essay competition.  From 1985 to 1989 he was a Sloan Fellow. In 1993 he was awarded the Xanthopoulos Prize. He has been a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] since 2001,<ref> {{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2001&unit_id=&institution=|title=APS Fellow Archive|publisher=APS|access-date=18 September 2020}} </ref> Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] since 2010, and [[Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] since 2013. In 2025 he was awarded the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)]].<ref>[https://www.ictp.it/news/2025/8/2025-ictp-dirac-medal-goes-gravity-explorers Dirac Medal (ICTP) 2025]</ref>
